question.:question/problem:
Let $C$ be the section of $y=3 x + 1$ between its intersections with the horizontal lines $y=4$ and $y=7$.

Which definite integral is equivalent to

$$
\int_C \left(y e^{x}\right)\,\mathrm{d}s
$$

using $x=t$? Do not evaluate the integral.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First solve the intersection equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}3 x + 1=4&\implies x=1\\
3 x + 1=7&\implies x=2\end{aligned}
$$

Set $x=t$. Parametrize the curve by

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle t,3 t + 1\rangle,\qquad 1\le t\le 2.
$$

Differentiate both coordinates and take the magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r\,\!{}^{\prime}(t)&=\langle 1,3\rangle,\\
\|\mathbf r\,\!{}^{\prime}(t)\|&=\sqrt{1+\left(3\right)^2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute both coordinates into the scalar function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf r(t))&=\left(3 t + 1\right) e^{t}\\
&=\left(3 t + 1\right) e^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiply the scalar by the speed and use the parameter bounds:

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_{1}^{2} f(\mathbf r(t))\|\mathbf r\,\!{}^{\prime}(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Thus the required setup is

$$
\int_{1}^{2}\left(\left(3 t + 1\right) e^{t}\right)\,\sqrt{1+\left(3\right)^2}\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Evaluate $\nabla\cdot\mathbf F$ at the point $(1,0)$.

For $\mathbf F=P\,\mathbf i+Q\,\mathbf j$, use

$$

Differentiate before evaluating at the point. The other coordinate is held constant in each derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla\cdot\mathbf F
&=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\ln(x+2y)+\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(xe^{2y})\\
&=\frac{1}{x+2y}+2xe^{2y}.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
(\nabla\cdot\mathbf F)(1,0)

Evaluate $\nabla\cdot\mathbf F$ at the point $(2,1)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The divergence is a scalar:

$$
\nabla\cdot\mathbf F=\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}.
$$

Both components require the product rule. In the first derivative, hold $y$ constant and use $\partial(xy)/\partial x=y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}
&=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(xe^{xy})\\
&=e^{xy}+xye^{xy}.
\end{aligned}
$$

In the second derivative, hold $x$ constant and differentiate the logarithm using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}
&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\bigl(y\ln(x+y)\bigr)\\
&=\ln(x+y)+\frac{y}{x+y}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Add the derivatives before substituting. Since $2+1>0$, the point lies in the domain:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla\cdot\mathbf F
&=(1+xy)e^{xy}+\ln(x+y)+\frac{y}{x+y},\\
(\nabla\cdot\mathbf F)(2,1)
&=(1+2\cdot1)e^{2\cdot1}+\ln(2+1)+\frac{1}{2+1}\\

\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the outward flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y)=(x^3+y)\,\mathbf i+(x+y)\,\mathbf j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf r(t)=2\cos t\,\mathbf i+\sin t\,\mathbf j$ for $0\leq t\leq 2\pi$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The parametrization traverses $C$ once counterclockwise, so the outward flux is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Phi&=\oint_C P\,\mathrm{d}y-Q\,\mathrm{d}x\\
&=\int_0^{2\pi}(P y'-Q x')\,\mathrm{d}t.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $P$ and $Q$ are evaluated at $(x(t),y(t))$.

Along $C$, $x=2\cos t$ and $y=\sin t$, so

$$
\begin{aligned}
P&=8\cos^3t+\sin t, & Q&=2\cos t+\sin t,\\
x'(t)&=-2\sin t, & y'(t)&=\cos t.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus

$$
\begin{aligned}
P y'-Q x'&=(8\cos^3t+\sin t)\cos t\\
&\quad-(2\cos t+\sin t)(-2\sin t)\\
&=8\cos^4t+5\sin t\cos t+2\sin^2t.
\end{aligned}
$$

Reduce the fourth power by applying the cosine double-angle identity twice:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\cos^4t&=\left(\frac{1+\cos(2t)}2\right)^2\\
&=\frac14\left(1+2\cos(2t)+\frac{1+\cos(4t)}2\right)\\
&=\frac{3+4\cos(2t)+\cos(4t)}8.
\end{aligned}
$$

Also, $2\sin^2t=1-\cos(2t)$ and $5\sin t\cos t=\frac52\sin(2t)$. Substituting and collecting terms gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Phi&=\int_0^{2\pi}\left(4+3\cos(2t)+\cos(4t)+\frac52\sin(2t)\right)\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=\left[4t+\frac32\sin(2t)+\frac14\sin(4t)-\frac54\cos(2t)\right]_0^{2\pi}\\
&=\left(8\pi-\frac54\right)-\left(-\frac54\right)=8\pi.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the outward flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y)=(x+y)\,\mathbf i+(x+2y)\,\mathbf j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf r(t)=2\cos t\,\mathbf i+\sin t\,\mathbf j$ for $0\leq t\leq 2\pi$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The parametrization traverses $C$ once counterclockwise, so the outward flux is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Phi&=\oint_C P\,\mathrm{d}y-Q\,\mathrm{d}x\\
&=\int_0^{2\pi}(P y'-Q x')\,\mathrm{d}t.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $P$ and $Q$ are evaluated at $(x(t),y(t))$.

Along $C$, $x=2\cos t$ and $y=\sin t$, so

$$
\begin{aligned}
P&=2\cos t+\sin t, & Q&=2\cos t+2\sin t,\\
x'(t)&=-2\sin t, & y'(t)&=\cos t.
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute into the flux integrand and collect terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P y'-Q x'&=(2\cos t+\sin t)\cos t\\
&\quad-(2\cos t+2\sin t)(-2\sin t)\\
&=2\cos^2t+5\sin t\cos t+4\sin^2t.
\end{aligned}
$$

The squared terms have different coefficients, so their sum is not constant. Use $\cos^2t=(1+\cos(2t))/2$, $\sin^2t=(1-\cos(2t))/2$, and $\sin t\cos t=\sin(2t)/2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Phi&=\int_0^{2\pi}\left(3-\cos(2t)+\frac52\sin(2t)\right)\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=\left[3t-\frac12\sin(2t)-\frac54\cos(2t)\right]_0^{2\pi}\\
&=\left(6\pi-\frac54\right)-\left(-\frac54\right)=6\pi.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the outward flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y)=(y-x)\,\mathbf i-(x+y)\,\mathbf j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf r(t)=2\cos t\,\mathbf i+2\sin t\,\mathbf j$ for $0\leq t\leq 2\pi$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The parametrization traverses $C$ once counterclockwise, so the outward flux is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Phi&=\oint_C P\,\mathrm{d}y-Q\,\mathrm{d}x\\
&=\int_0^{2\pi}(P y'-Q x')\,\mathrm{d}t.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $P$ and $Q$ are evaluated at $(x(t),y(t))$.

Along $C$, substitute $x=2\cos t$ and $y=2\sin t$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P&=2\sin t-2\cos t, & Q&=-2\cos t-2\sin t,\\
x'(t)&=-2\sin t, & y'(t)&=2\cos t.
\end{aligned}
$$

The two mixed terms cancel. Using $\cos^2t+\sin^2t=1$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
P y'-Q x'&=(2\sin t-2\cos t)(2\cos t)\\
&\quad-(-2\cos t-2\sin t)(-2\sin t)\\
&=-4\cos^2t-4\sin^2t=-4.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\Phi=\int_0^{2\pi}-4\,\mathrm{d}t=[-4t]_0^{2\pi}=-8\pi.
$$

The negative sign means that the net flow is inward.

The curve $C$ is parameterized by $\mathbf r(t)=(- 2 t)\,\mathbf i+(- t)\,\mathbf j$, $0\le t\le 2$. Calculate the flux of $\mathbf F(x,y)=(4)\,\mathbf i+(-3)\,\mathbf j$ through $C$ with respect to the unit normal $\mathbf n$ shown. Gray field arrows indicate direction only.

*Hint:* Check the pictured normal against the tangent for increasing $t$. For a clockwise normal use $$
\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds=\int_a^b(Py\prime-Qx\prime)\,\mathrm dt.
$$
For an anticlockwise normal, negate this expression.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the supplied parameterization $x=- 2 t,\ y=- t$, $0\le t\le 2$. It runs from $(0,0)$ to $(-4,-2)$.

The tangent has direction $(-2,-1)$. The pictured normal is its $90^\circ$ anticlockwise rotation, with direction $(1,-2)$.

![Tangent and selected normal](images/ea/eaf9df468563558c596a3ef20c8150cab92f40a3f0db52cdb2ccf7ef0a85720d.png)

Substitute the curve into the field and differentiate its coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x(t),y(t))&=4 \\
Q(x(t),y(t))&=-3 \\
x'&=-2 \\
y'&=-1\end{aligned}
$$

The clockwise formula has the opposite normal, so negate it for the selected normal.

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds&=-\int_{0}^{2}(Py\prime-Qx\prime)\,\mathrm dt \\
&=-\int_{0}^{2}\left[(4)(-1)-(-3)(-2)\right]\,\mathrm dt \\
&=\int_{0}^{2}(10)\,\mathrm dt \\
&=\left[10 t\right]_{0}^{2} \\
&=(20)-(0) \\
&=20\end{aligned}
$$
